extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, and practitioners interested in building construction and aesthetic principles
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic principles for designing protective buildings (walls, roofs, apertures) from foundation upward, with guidance on materials, structural members, and ornamentation. Emphasises constructive necessity first, then appropriate decoration chosen by the builder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold practical duty of buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings have either (1) to hold and protect something, or (2) to place or carry something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this functional division to classify architectural works (protective architecture includes churches, houses, treasuries, fortresses, dykes; position architecture includes bridges, aqueducts, lighthouses, chimneys, staircases, towers). Design and evaluation should begin from the building's primary practical duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical/Design approach: construct from foundation upwards
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead the builder from foundation upward so he may discover the best way of doing everything and, having discovered it, never forget it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide materials and tools (stones, bricks, chisels, trowels) and help only when puzzled; allow the builder freedom to choose ornaments after the construction is rightly found; counteract previous prejudices but avoid imposing ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective architecture divided into walls, roofs, apertures
rubrics_metrics.description: Protective architecture has to wall a space, to roof it, and to give access to it (persons, light, and air); therefore consider walls, roofs, and apertures as its three principal divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the connection of these members generally, then examine each in detail. Flooring/paving are only architecture when also acting as a roof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wall must respond to vertical and lateral pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: A wall is an even and united fence which often sustains vertical or lateral pressure; its strength increases by thickness, or by gathering into piers (for vertical pressure) or supporting by buttresses (for lateral pressure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If required mainly to resist roof/vertical pressure it becomes piers; if lateral pressure is slight retain wall character with buttresses at intervals; if lateral pressure is great it becomes a continuous buttress (dyke/rampart). Design form should follow the pressure conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design sequence for walls: wall -> piers -> buttresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Study (A) the general idea and right construction of walls; (B) how the wall is gathered into piers and the right construction of piers; (C) how a wall is supported by buttresses and the right construction of buttresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this ordered examination to ensure correct decisions about wall members and their interrelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roofs: study sectional forms first, then expanded forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A roof is the covering of a space; study forms as carried over a narrow section, then expand these along a width to produce vaults, domes, gabled roofs, spires, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider arched vs gabled sections: arched sections give vaulted roofs and domes; gabled sections give gabled roofs and spires. Prepare lintels/arches over piers as necessary before true roofing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apertures: determine shape, filling, and external protection
rubrics_metrics.description: For doors or windows determine (1) the proper shape of the entire aperture; (2) the way it is to be filled (valves or glass); (3) modes of protecting it outside and fitting appliances of convenience (porches, balconies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The character of intervals between piers is determined by pier character; treat apertures as structural and functional components, not merely decorative holes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wall composition: three necessary members (Base, Veil/Body, Cornice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial walls in their perfect form have three distinct members: the Foundation (Base), Body or 'Veil', and Cornice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part has distinct functions: base spreads and makes visible the foundation, veil is the even portion responsible for enclosure/privacy, cornice protects from weather or prepares to carry weight. They should 'grow out of each other' and form a coherent whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation/Base must be visible and spread load
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation (base) should be visible to the eye and form part of the structure above ground; it is a long foot, wider than the wall, which keeps it from settling into the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a firm, level foundation when possible but design assuming the building stands on ground capable of yielding; use tiered large stones with breadth decreasing upwards and employ binding stones across joints for security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wall veil (body) should be of equal thickness and appropriately coursed
rubrics_metrics.description: The body or 'veil' is the even portion of a wall; if of equal thickness it is a proper wall; where localized thickness occurs that is a pier or buttress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use moderate wall thickness with strengthening piers or buttresses; when materials are loose or ill-shaped, introduce courses of more solid material (coursing) and string courses at regular heights for structural strength and to express internal divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coursing and string-courses strengthen and decorate walls
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce courses of more solid material (stone bands) in walls of imperfect material; string-courses act as epochs in the wall's existence, often corresponding to internal stories and expressing structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coursing has both constructive and decorative weight: it is often better to strengthen imperfect walls by carefully laid stone courses than by increasing thickness; decorative reasons for coursing are significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masonry must not call undue attention to itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Masonry is bad which appears to have arrested the attention of the architect more than absolute conditions of strength require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid affectation: do not studiously conceal or studiously display masonry beyond necessity. Exhibited masonry often covers up inability to fill blank spaces. Divisions are right when necessary and wrong when thrust upon attention as mere divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walls should appear 'living' with members and purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: A wall ought to have members in its make and purposes in its existence like an organized creature; it should answer its ends in a living and energetic way rather than be 'dead'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plain, lifeless walls; give walls clear members (base, veil, cornice) and purposeful form so they are felt to be 'sweet and lovely' rather than mere partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume ground yield — design for some settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: In reasoning upon superstructure, assume the building stands on ground capable of yielding in some degree to its weight and design accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume perfect invisible foundations; base design should accommodate settlement over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base formation: tiered large stones, receding breadth, and seats
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare the base with large stones laid over a larger width than the wall, possibly in tiers with breadth decreasing each tier, and consider widening lower ledge into a stone seat for effect and protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In important positions, bevel and decorate lower ledges; variations correspond to decorative needs and building disposition but the solid base type is frequently followed in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cornice functions: roof to the wall or hand to carry weight
rubrics_metrics.description: A cornice has one of two offices: if wall carries nothing above, the cornice acts as roof to defend from weather; if there is superincumbent weight, the cornice is expanded to carry that weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cornices to distribute weather and load — include a projecting flat stone and a sloped or supporting stone beneath (X and Y stones). Ensure the projecting element is supported so edges will not break off; relate cornice design to base by analogy (hand vs foot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical cornice detailing (X and Y stones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a bevelled/sloping stone (X) beneath a projecting upright-edged stone (Y) to form a stable cornice that protects the wall and receives superincumbent weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thin the projecting stone where unnecessary thickness exists; ensure lower stones correspond to base elements and that the cornice properly distributes loads into the wall veil beneath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt construction details to local materials and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The general structural types are subject to many modifications according to circumstances (exposure, available materials, need for cellars or underground rooms, decorative requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviations from ideal forms are often justified by necessity; however, be wary of mistaken decorative deviations and prefer structural correctness when possible.
